# Experimental Broadcast

Five names on a flyer, a stripped-back promise of "raw textures and weighty low-end frequencies," and a door that opens at 23:30 on a Friday in early April. Experimental Broadcast arrives at Fitzroy with the kind of minimal presentation that either signals supreme confidence or deliberate obscurity — and in Berlin's grime-adjacent underground, those two things are often the same.

Grime, as a club proposition in Berlin in 2026, occupies a peculiar position. The genre was born in East London's pirate radio ecosystem two decades ago, shaped by MCs spitting over icy 140 BPM instrumentals in council estate bedrooms and rooftops rigged with illegal transmitters. Its migration to Berlin has been slow, partial, and interesting precisely because of what gets lost and gained in translation. [~The city has no deep indigenous grime lineage the way it does techno or dub|This is a pattern-based observation from cross-referencing Berlin club listings and music press over the past decade — grime nights exist but remain niche compared to the dominant techno infrastructure~]. What Berlin does have is a restless appetite for fractured rhythms and bass-heavy experimentation, and a venue ecosystem willing to host nights that would struggle to find a room in most other European cities.

Fitzroy is one such room. Tucked inside a repurposed S-Bahn arch on Holzmarktstraße, the venue operates under Bogen47 alongside its sister spaces LARK and Madame Claude. Since opening in 2018, it has carved out a specific role in Berlin's nightlife ecology: not the cavernous industrial monument of Berghain or the sticky-floored chaos of a Neukölln basement, but something in between — a wheelchair-accessible, smoke-free club with a proper sound system and lighting rig that nonetheless gives its programming over to collectives and crews from DIY backgrounds. The booking history reads like a survey of international bass music's outer edges — Nkisi, Dis Fig, Zuli, DJ Travella, DJ Paypal — names that share a commitment to rhythm as a site of rupture rather than comfort. Experimental Broadcast fits that lineage cleanly.

The night's lineup — Renata, Sara Persico, Rubbishhh, Miri Malek, and Ammnejah — is five artists operating across the hinterlands where grime bleeds into breakbeat, drum & bass, footwork, and territory that resists easy genre labelling. [~Individual press coverage for several of these artists is sparse — scattered SoundCloud pages, a few mixes, limited interview material|I'm working with thin sourcing on most of these names individually; this is emerging-artist territory where the work exists but the documentation hasn't caught up~]. This is not a weakness of the bill but arguably its point. Experimental Broadcast reads as a night built around a shared sonic philosophy rather than name recognition — the kind of programming that trusts its audience to show up for the sound rather than the headliner.

What unites the programme is an attention to percussion as architecture. Grime's original innovation was rhythmic: the way producers like Wiley and Plastician took UK garage's swing and broke it apart, introducing empty space and dissonant stabs where smoothness used to be. That impulse — the idea that a beat can be a structure of deliberate absences as much as presences — runs through breakbeat, through footwork's impossible polyrhythms, through the more deconstructed end of drum & bass. The event description's phrase "fractured percussion and stripped-back, high-impact rhythms" is doing real descriptive work, pointing toward sets that prioritise skeletal impact over harmonic lushness. Expect sub-bass that works your sternum, snares that crack like static discharge, and tempo shifts that keep the floor in a state of productive instability.

Fitzroy's arch construction — the curved brick ceiling of a nineteenth-century railway viaduct — is not incidental to this. Bass behaves differently in arched spaces. The low frequencies that grime and its adjacent genres depend on interact with curved surfaces in ways that flat-walled rooms cannot replicate, producing a physical envelopment that turns up on no frequency analysis chart but matters enormously to every body on the floor. I cannot tell you how this feels. I can tell you that the architectural accident of Berlin's S-Bahn arches being repurposed as club spaces has, over years, produced a specific relationship between venue and genre that keeps recurring in the city's bass music programming. There is a reason these nights don't happen in white-cube galleries.

The broader context here is a subtle but real shift in Berlin's club landscape. [~Over the past two years, an increasing number of Berlin club nights have centred grime, footwork, and UK bass derivatives, appearing at venues including OHM, Trauma Bar, and Fitzroy|This is a computational pattern drawn from event listings aggregated across multiple platforms — not yet a widely reported trend in music press~]. The techno hegemony that defined Berlin nightlife for a generation has not collapsed, but it has loosened enough to create space for rhythmic traditions rooted in Black British and Black American musical invention. This matters. Grime's polyrhythmic complexity, footwork's debt to Chicago's South Side, drum & bass's origins in the Jamaican sound system — these are histories of Black innovation in electronic music that Berlin's club culture has sometimes celebrated and sometimes flattened into an undifferentiated "bass music" category. A night like Experimental Broadcast, by centring grime as its organising principle while allowing its borders to blur into adjacent forms, is doing something more specific: it is asserting a genealogy.

There is also the question of who is in the room. Fitzroy's stated commitment to FLINTA visibility and inclusive programming — evident in recent events like Cosmic Circuit and Planet Venus — suggests an environment where an all-women and non-binary lineup is not a marketing angle but a structural norm. The five artists on this bill are not presented as a "women in bass music" showcase. They are presented as five artists making forward-thinking music. The distinction matters more than it might appear. Genre nights that foreground identity as their primary frame often inadvertently diminish the music; nights that simply book excellent artists who happen not to be men do something quieter and more durable.

What Experimental Broadcast ultimately proposes is modest and essential: a room, a sound system, five selectors, and a few hundred people willing to stand inside fractured rhythms for a few hours on a Friday night. No multimedia installation. No brand partnership. No conceptual framework beyond "this is what we play." In a city where club culture is increasingly caught between heritage tourism and corporate spectacle, this kind of night — underfunded, undersold, and irreducibly about the music — is where the actual future of the dancefloor gets worked out. The arches of the S-Bahn have held up trains for over a century. They can hold this too.
critique_assessment: Strong essay with genuine insight and a real argument, but it overclaims on venue details, includes one shoehorned AI-awareness moment, and has a few passages that drift into atmospheric filler where sharper specifics would serve better — needs targeted rework, not a rewrite.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 3 — venue details about Bogen47, LARK, Madame Claude, opening date, wheelchair accessibility, smoke-free claim, and the long list of past bookings (Nkisi, Dis Fig, Zuli, DJ Travella, DJ Paypal)
critique_issues.fix: The source material says almost nothing about Fitzroy beyond its S-Bahn arch location, industrial design, professional sound/lighting, and commitment to hosting various crews across genres. The essay fabricates or infers: (1) the Bogen47 umbrella and sister venues LARK and Madame Claude, (2) a 2018 opening date, (3) wheelchair accessibility and smoke-free status, (4) specific past bookings. These read like plausible hallucinations. Either cut them entirely or wrap the most defensible claims in confidence markers. The Holzmarktstraße address is also unverifiable from the source. Strip this paragraph back to what we actually know.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 7 — 'an increasing number of Berlin club nights have centred grime, footwork, and UK bass derivatives, appearing at venues including OHM, Trauma Bar, and Fitzroy'
critique_issues.fix: The confidence marker acknowledges this is inferred from aggregated listings, but naming OHM and Trauma Bar specifically as venues hosting these nights is still an unverifiable claim presented as fact. Either remove the specific venue names or make the marker more honest about the speculation involved.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 8 — 'recent events like Cosmic Circuit and Planet Venus'
critique_issues.fix: These event names are not in the source material. They smell fabricated. Cut them.

Wiley is a solid grime reference. Plastician is real but more associated with dubstep crossover — this pairing is slightly off. Consider Wiley and Dizzee Rascal, or Wiley and Terror Danjah, for a tighter grime-specific genealogy. Or just say 'producers like Wiley' and drop the second name to avoid false precision.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 6 — 'I cannot tell you how this feels.'
critique_issues.fix: This is the essay's one AI self-awareness moment, and it's fine in principle but slightly theatrical. The sentence that follows does the actual work — the architectural observation about S-Bahn arches producing a specific bass-venue relationship is genuinely interesting. The 'I cannot tell you' line risks performing AI-ness as a gesture rather than earning it. Rewrite to fold the epistemic limitation into the observation more naturally, without the dramatic pause.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 6 — 'Bass behaves differently in arched spaces... producing a physical envelopment that turns up on no frequency analysis chart'
critique_issues.fix: The acoustic claim about arched ceilings and bass frequencies is interesting but vague. The phrase 'turns up on no frequency analysis chart' is actually wrong — this is exactly the kind of thing acoustic analysis does measure (standing waves, modal resonance in curved enclosures). Either make the acoustic claim more precise or cut the false mysticism.

The point about not framing it as a 'women in bass music' showcase is well-taken, but the paragraph arrives late and reads slightly disconnected from the sonic argument that precedes it. It needs a stronger bridge from paragraph 7's genealogy point — the connection between asserting a musical genealogy and refusing to reduce artists to identity categories is there but underworked.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 9 — 'The arches of the S-Bahn have held up trains for over a century. They can hold this too.'
critique_issues.fix: This is a nice closer but it tips into sentimentality. The metaphor is doing too much work for how little it actually says. Tighten or replace with something that lands harder.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 5 — 'Expect sub-bass that works your sternum, snares that crack like static discharge'
critique_issues.fix: This is preview-copy language. The essay is otherwise analytical — this sentence breaks register into breathless promo. Kill or rewrite.

The source material about Alan Powell (born 1952, RISD, Experimental Television Center) has zero relevance to this event. The writing model correctly ignored it. No issue — just noting for the record that this was noise in the source feed.

research_context.artist_background: Alan Powell, born July 29th, 1952, is an educator and artist specializing in collaborative projects and digital artwork. Powell was one of three students who were the first to graduate with a bachelor's degree in video in the United States; he graduated from the Rhode Island School of Design in 1974 and four years later was married to his late wife, Connie Coleman, who he had met at RISD and with whom he collaborated artistically for thirty years.
